topics.title: Location of Africa on the Map of the World

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: A continent
questions.a: A continent is a very large mass of land on the earth's surface.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: A line of latitude
questions.a: A line of latitude is an imaginary line running east to west, showing how far a place is north or south of the Equator.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: An island
questions.a: An island is a piece of land completely surrounded by water.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: A capital city
questions.a: A capital city is the city where the government of a country is based.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: The two largest continents in the world.
questions.a: Asia and Africa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: The four oceans of the world.
questions.a: Atlantic Ocean, Pacific Ocean, Indian Ocean and Arctic Ocean.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: The six regions of Africa.
questions.a: Northern Africa, West Africa, East Africa, Central Africa, Southern Africa and the Horn of Africa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: Any three island countries of Africa.
questions.a: Any three of: Madagascar, Seychelles, Mauritius, Comoros, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: The four countries of the Horn of Africa.
questions.a: Ethiopia, Somalia, Djibouti and Eritrea.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: The line of latitude that divides the earth into two equal halves.
questions.a: The Equator.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: The ocean found to the west of Africa.
questions.a: The Atlantic Ocean.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: The sea that separates Africa from Europe.
questions.a: The Mediterranean Sea.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: The largest island in Africa.
questions.a: Madagascar.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: The region of Africa in which Uganda is found.
questions.a: East Africa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: Why is Africa described as the only continent crossed by the Equator, both Tropics and the Prime Meridian?
questions.a: Because Africa stretches from about 37°N to about 35°S and from about 17°W to about 51°E. This spread means the Equator crosses its middle, the Tropic of Cancer crosses the north, the Tropic of Capricorn crosses the south, and the Prime Meridian passes through West Africa. No other continent is crossed by all four.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: Why are lines of latitude and longitude important on a map?
questions.a: They help us find the exact position of a place on a map. Latitude gives the distance north or south of the Equator, and longitude gives the distance east or west of the Prime Meridian. Where the two lines cross is the position of the place.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: A ship sails from Mombasa in Kenya to Lagos in Nigeria. Name the ocean it starts from and the ocean it ends in.
questions.a: It starts in the Indian Ocean (Mombasa is on the east coast) and ends in the Atlantic Ocean (Lagos is on the west coast).

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: Draw an outline map of Africa. On it, mark and label the Equator, the Tropic of Cancer and Uganda.
questions.a: Learner's map. It should show an outline of Africa with a horizontal line through the middle labelled Equator, a horizontal line north of it labelled Tropic of Cancer, and Uganda marked in East Africa on the Equator.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: Give one reason why Tanzania's capital is Dodoma and not Dar es Salaam, its largest city.
questions.a: Dodoma was chosen as the capital because it lies in the centre of the country, which makes it easier to reach from all parts of Tanzania. Dar es Salaam remains the largest city and main port.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Africa on the Map of the World
questions.q: Kampala is at about 0° latitude. What does this tell you about Uganda's position on the earth?
questions.a: It shows that Uganda lies on the Equator, so part of the country is in the Northern Hemisphere and part is in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Physical features
questions.a: Physical features are the land forms that exist on the earth's surface and give the land its shape.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A plateau
questions.a: A plateau is a large area of fairly flat land raised high above the land around it.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A delta
questions.a: A delta is the fan-shaped area of flat land formed where a river deposits soil as it enters a lake or a sea through several channels.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A rift valley
questions.a: A rift valley is a long, deep, steep-sided valley formed when the land between two parallel faults sinks.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any three fold mountains or ranges in Africa.
questions.a: Atlas Mountains, Cape Ranges, and the folded ridges of the Atlas system in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any three volcanic mountains in Africa.
questions.a: Any three of: Mt Kilimanjaro, Mt Cameroon, Mt Elgon, Mt Kenya, Tibesti, Ahaggar.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The three deserts of Africa named in this topic.
questions.a: The Sahara Desert, the Kalahari Desert and the Namib Desert.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any four man-made lakes in Africa and the dams that formed them.
questions.a: Lake Nasser — Aswan High Dam; Lake Volta — Akosombo Dam; Lake Kariba — Kariba Dam; Lake Kainji — Kainji Dam.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The longest river in Africa.
questions.a: The River Nile.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The deepest lake in Africa.
questions.a: Lake Tanganyika.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The river on which Victoria Falls is found.
questions.a: The River Zambezi.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The sea into which the River Nile pours its water.
questions.a: The Mediterranean Sea.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The largest lake in Africa.
questions.a: Lake Victoria.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: How are fault-block mountains formed?
questions.a: The land cracks along two parallel faults. The block of land between the cracks is pushed upwards, or the land on either side sinks, leaving the middle block standing high as a mountain.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give two reasons why the water level of Lake Chad has been falling.
questions.a: Long droughts with little rainfall, and too much water being taken from the rivers that feed it for irrigation. (Also: silting and the growth of the population around it.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why do many rivers in Africa have waterfalls and rapids?
questions.a: Because most of Africa is a plateau. Where a river leaves the high plateau and drops towards the coast, the sudden fall in the land makes waterfalls and rapids.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A trader wants to send goods by water from Kinshasa to Europe. Name the river and the ocean the goods will pass through.
questions.a: The River Congo, then the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give two ways in which mountains help the people who live near them, and one way they make life difficult.
questions.a: Help: they receive relief rainfall for farming, have fertile volcanic soils, attract tourists, and are sources of rivers. Difficulty: they make the building of roads and railways hard and expensive (steep slopes also cause soil erosion and landslides).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why is the Namib Desert dry although it lies along the coast?
questions.a: Because the cold Benguela ocean current flows along that coast. Air passing over cold water carries little moisture, so very little rain falls on the land.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw the map of Africa and mark on it the River Niger, Lake Chad and the Atlas Mountains.
questions.a: Learner's map. The Niger should be shown in West Africa flowing into the Gulf of Guinea, Lake Chad in the middle of West/Central Africa, and the Atlas Mountains in the far north-west.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Weather
questions.a: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere of a place at a particular time.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Climate
questions.a: Climate is the average weather conditions of a place recorded over a long period of time.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Desertification
questions.a: Desertification is the spread of desert conditions into land that was not desert before.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A rain shadow
questions.a: A rain shadow is the dry leeward side of a mountain, which receives little rainfall because the moist air lost its water on the windward side.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any four elements of weather and the instrument used to measure each.
questions.a: Rainfall — rain gauge; temperature — thermometer; wind direction — wind vane; wind speed — anemometer. (Also humidity — hygrometer; air pressure — barometer.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The six climatic regions of Africa.
questions.a: Equatorial, Tropical (savannah), Desert, Mediterranean, Temperate and Montane.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The three hot deserts of Africa.
questions.a: The Sahara, the Kalahari and the Namib.
accepted: The Sahara, the Kalahari and the Namib.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any three factors that influence the climate of Africa.
questions.a: Any three of: latitude, altitude, nearness to water bodies, winds, ocean currents, relief, vegetation, human activities, land mass.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The type of climate that has hot dry summers and warm wet winters.
questions.a: The Mediterranean climate.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: One country in Africa with a Mediterranean climate.
questions.a: Any one of: Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt or South Africa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The ocean current that makes the Namib Desert dry.
questions.a: The cold Benguela Current.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The type of rainfall received on the windward slopes of Mt Rwenzori.
questions.a: Relief rainfall (orographic rainfall).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The dry dusty wind that blows over West Africa.
questions.a: The Harmattan.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why is it cold on top of Mt Kilimanjaro although it is near the Equator?
questions.a: Because temperature falls as altitude increases — by about 1 °C for every 150 metres. Kilimanjaro is 5,895 m high, so the top is far colder than the plains below, cold enough for ice and snow.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give three ways in which human activities have changed the climate of Africa.
questions.a: Cutting down forests reduces rainfall; burning bushes and using vehicles and factories releases gases that warm the earth; draining swamps reduces the moisture that goes into the air. (Overgrazing and mining also expose the soil.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why do desert areas become very cold at night?
questions.a: Deserts have clear skies and no clouds or water vapour to hold the heat. During the day the ground heats quickly, but at night the heat escapes fast into the sky, so it becomes very cold.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A farmer in northern Uganda complains that the rains now come late and stop early. Give two possible causes and two things the community can do about it.
questions.a: Causes: cutting down of trees and swamp drainage in the area, and wider climate change caused by global warming. Actions: plant trees (afforestation and reafforestation), protect the remaining wetlands and forests, practise agroforestry, and harvest rain water for irrigation.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why do people in the Sahara practise irrigation farming instead of rain-fed farming?
questions.a: Because the desert receives less than 250 mm of rain a year, which is too little for crops. Irrigation brings water from rivers, oases or underground so that crops can grow.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A place records a temperature of 24 °C at sea level. About what temperature would you expect 1,500 metres up the same mountain? Show your working.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw the map of Africa and shade the equatorial climate region.
questions.a: Learner's map. The equatorial region should be shaded as a belt along the Equator, covering the Congo Basin and the coast of West Africa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Vegetation
questions.a: Vegetation is all the plants that grow in an area — trees, shrubs, grass and herbs.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Natural vegetation
questions.a: Natural vegetation is vegetation that grows on its own without being planted by people.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A game park
questions.a: A game park is a large area of land set aside by government where wild animals are protected in their natural home.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Poaching
questions.a: Poaching is the illegal killing of wild animals.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any five types of vegetation found in Africa.
questions.a: Any five of: equatorial forest, savannah, mangrove forest, Mediterranean vegetation, temperate grasslands (velds), desert and semi-desert vegetation, montane vegetation, swamp vegetation.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any three factors that influence vegetation distribution.
questions.a: Any three of: climate, type of soil, relief/altitude, drainage, human activities.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any four animals found in the savannah.
questions.a: Any four of: lions, elephants, giraffes, zebras, antelopes, buffaloes, leopards, rhinos.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any three game parks in Africa and the countries where they are found.
questions.a: Any three, for example: Murchison Falls — Uganda; Serengeti — Tanzania; Maasai Mara — Kenya; Kruger — South Africa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The type of vegetation found in the Congo Basin.
questions.a: Equatorial (tropical rain) forest.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The name given to the temperate grasslands of South Africa.
questions.a: The veld.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: One type of vegetation found along muddy sea coasts.
questions.a: Mangrove forest.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The vegetation zone with the largest number of big wild animals.
questions.a: The savannah.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: One reason why deserts have very few people.
questions.a: There is too little water and pasture; the heat is extreme and the soils are poor.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give four uses of vegetation to people.
questions.a: Vegetation gives timber, firewood and charcoal; it attracts rainfall; it prevents soil erosion; it is a home for wild animals; it attracts tourists; it provides medicine, food and raw materials for industry. (Any four.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why do animals live in different vegetation zones?
questions.a: Because each animal looks for the food, water, shelter and climate that suit it. Grass eaters stay where there is grass, leaf and fruit eaters stay in the forest, and animals that hunt follow the animals they feed on. Some also move away from people.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give three problems faced by game parks in Africa.
questions.a: Any three of: poaching, bush fires, drought, encroachment by farmers and herders, animal diseases, insecurity, limited funds, conflict with neighbouring communities.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A district has cut down most of its trees for charcoal. State two effects this will have and two solutions the district should adopt.
questions.a: Effects: rainfall will reduce and the area may face drought; the bare soil will suffer erosion and lose fertility. Solutions: start afforestation and reafforestation programmes; promote energy-saving stoves, biogas and agroforestry, and enforce laws against illegal cutting of trees.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why is the equatorial forest region sparsely populated although it receives plenty of rainfall?
questions.a: Because the forest is thick and hard to clear, the soils are leached by heavy rain and are not very fertile, transport is difficult, and there are many pests and diseases such as mosquitoes and tsetse flies.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give two reasons why mangrove trees can grow in salty water where other trees cannot.
questions.a: They have special stilt roots that hold them above the muddy water, and breathing roots that take in air. Their leaves and roots are also able to get rid of extra salt.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw the map of Africa and shade the savannah vegetation belt north of the Equator.
questions.a: Learner's map. The savannah belt should be shaded as a band lying between the equatorial forest and the Sahara Desert.

topics.title: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: An ethnic group
questions.a: An ethnic group is a large group of people who share the same origin, language family, customs and way of life.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: Migration
questions.a: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another to settle there.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: A cradle land
questions.a: A cradle land is the original home of a group of people before they migrated.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: A settlement pattern
questions.a: A settlement pattern is the way in which homes and villages are arranged in an area.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: Any four ethnic groups found in Africa.
questions.a: Any four of: Bantu, Nilotics, Nilo-Hamites, Cushites, Semites (Arabs), Berbers, Pygmies (Batwa), Bushmen (San).

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: Any three tribes belonging to the Bantu group.
questions.a: Any three of: Baganda, Banyankole, Bagisu, Bakiga, Kikuyu, Chagga, Zulu, Xhosa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: The three main settlement patterns.
questions.a: Nucleated (clustered), dispersed (scattered) and linear.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: Any four reasons why ethnic groups migrated from their cradle lands.
questions.a: Any four of: internal conflicts, wars, population increase, lack of enough land and water, harsh climate, expansionism, search for fertile soils and pasture, diseases and pests.
accepted: lack of enough land and water
search for fertile soils and pasture

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: The cradle land of the Bantu.
questions.a: The Congo–Cameroon region of West and Central Africa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: The cradle land of the Nilotics.
questions.a: Bahr-el-Ghazal in southern Sudan (South Sudan).

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: The ethnic group to which the Karimojong belong.
questions.a: The Nilo-Hamites (Plain Nilotes).

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: The ethnic group to which the Somali belong.
questions.a: The Cushites (Hamites).

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: The oldest known people of North Africa.
questions.a: The Berbers.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: Give four problems that the ethnic groups met during their migrations.
questions.a: Any four of: resistance from the indigenous people, difficulty in moving on foot over long distances, attacks by wild animals, diseases such as malaria and sleeping sickness, difficult terrain (forests, mountains, swamps, deserts), food and water shortage, harsh climate, language barriers.
accepted: difficulty in moving on foot over long distances
diseases such as malaria and sleeping sickness

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: Give three positive effects and two negative effects of the ethnic migrations.
questions.a: Positive: population increased; new skills and crops such as iron working and farming spread; intermarriages took place and new communities formed; trade developed; kingdoms were formed; languages spread. Negative: the indigenous people lost land; wars and conflicts broke out; cultures were changed or lost; diseases spread; lives and property were lost. (Any three and any two.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: Why did most migrating groups avoid thick forests and deserts?
questions.a: Because thick forests and deserts were difficult to travel through, had little food or pasture, and carried dangers such as wild animals, pests and shortage of water. Grasslands and river valleys offered water, pasture and easy movement.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: Many young people today leave the village for Kampala. Name this type of migration, give two reasons for it and two problems it causes in the town.
questions.a: It is rural–urban migration. Reasons: to look for jobs and better pay; to get better schools, hospitals and other services (also town attractions such as electricity). Problems in town: unemployment and crime; overcrowding, slums, pressure on housing, water and health services.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: A new group settles in an area where people already live. Give two things that may bring conflict and two things that may bring peaceful living together.
questions.a: Conflict: competition for land, water and pasture; differences in language and customs; loss of grazing land and cattle raids. Peaceful living: intermarriage and trade between the groups; sharing schools, markets and other services; learning one another's languages; respecting each other's culture and settling disputes through local leaders.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: Why do people in Karamoja often live in manyattas (homes built close together with a fence around them)?
questions.a: For security. Living close together behind one fence makes it easier to protect people and cattle from raiders and wild animals, and it helps the community share water and pasture.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: The People of Africa — Ethnic Groups and Settlement Patterns
questions.q: Draw the map of Africa and show, using arrows, the direction of the Bantu migration.
questions.a: Learner's map. Arrows should start from the Congo–Cameroon region and point eastwards into East Africa and southwards into Southern Africa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: An explorer
questions.a: An explorer is a person who travels to an unknown place in order to find out about it.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A colony
questions.a: A colony is a country or area ruled by a foreign power.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The Scramble for Africa
questions.a: The Scramble for Africa was the rush by European powers to take control of parts of Africa in the late 1800s.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Assimilation
questions.a: Assimilation was the French method of ruling colonies by making Africans adopt French language, culture and citizenship.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any four groups of foreigners who came to Africa.
questions.a: Any four of: Arab traders, Persian traders, Indian traders, European explorers, European traders, missionaries, colonialists, settlers.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any four European explorers and one thing each is remembered for.
questions.a: Any four, for example: Bartholomew Diaz — reached the Cape of Good Hope; Vasco da Gama — sailed to India round Africa; Mungo Park — explored the River Niger; David Livingstone — explored Central Africa and fought the slave trade; Speke and Grant — reached the source of the Nile.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any four European countries that colonised parts of Africa and one colony of each.
questions.a: Britain — Uganda; France — Senegal; Portugal — Angola; Belgium — Congo; Germany — Tanganyika; Italy — Libya. (Any four pairs.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The three items exchanged at each corner of the Triangular Trade.
questions.a: Europe to Africa — guns, cloth, beads and alcohol. Africa to America — enslaved people. America to Europe — sugar, cotton, tobacco and coffee.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The conference that partitioned Africa and the year it began.
questions.a: The Berlin Conference, which began in 1884 (1884–1885).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The two African countries that were not colonised.
questions.a: Ethiopia and Liberia.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The colonial power that used indirect rule.
questions.a: Britain.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The year Britain abolished the slave trade.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The battle where Ethiopia defeated the Italians.
questions.a: The Battle of Adowa, in 1896.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give four reasons why European explorers came to Africa.
questions.a: Any four of: to find the sources of the great rivers, to find a sea route to India, to map the interior, to look for raw materials and markets, to look for land for settlement, adventure and fame, to spread Christianity, to see how the slave trade could be stopped.
accepted: to find the sources of the great rivers
to find a sea route to India
to look for raw materials and markets
to look for land for settlement
to see how the slave trade could be stopped

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give four problems the explorers faced.
questions.a: Any four of: tropical diseases, attacks by hostile people, wild animals, difficult terrain, language barriers, shortage of food and clean water, poor transport, desertion by porters, harsh climate.
accepted: shortage of food and clean water

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give three causes and three effects of the Great Trek.
questions.a: Causes: dislike of British rule; the abolition of slavery in 1833; unfair compensation for freed slaves; the use of English instead of Dutch; the search for more land. Effects: the Boer republics of Transvaal, Orange Free State and Natal were founded; wars with African peoples such as the Zulu; Africans lost land; minerals were discovered inland; the Anglo-Boer wars followed; apartheid attitudes took root. (Any three each.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give two political, two economic and two social effects of foreign influence in Africa.
questions.a: Political: Africans lost independence; traditional rulers lost power; new boundaries split tribes. Economic: raw materials were exploited; roads, railways and towns were built; new cash crops and taxes were introduced. Social: Christianity and Islam spread; schools and hospitals were started; African culture was distorted and foreign languages introduced. (Any two each.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why did some African leaders collaborate with Europeans while others resisted?
questions.a: Some collaborated because they wanted guns, protection against stronger neighbours, trade goods, or a stronger position for their own kingdom, and some did not understand the treaties they signed. Others resisted because they wanted to keep their independence, their land, their cattle and their culture, and because they saw the foreigners as invaders.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The borders drawn in Berlin were straight lines. Explain two problems this has caused Africa up to today.
questions.a: The straight borders split single tribes between two or more countries (for example, the Maasai between Kenya and Tanzania), which weakens communities and causes cross-border problems. They also joined together groups that had never lived together, which has led to conflict, and they left some countries landlocked with no coastline of their own.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw the map of Africa and shade the areas that were ruled by Britain and by France.
questions.a: Learner's map. British areas should include Egypt, Sudan, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, Zimbabwe and South Africa; French areas should include most of West Africa (Senegal, Mali, Niger, Ivory Coast, Chad) and Algeria.

topics.title: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Pan-Africanism
questions.a: Pan-Africanism is the feeling and movement of uniting all African people and promoting the political, economic and social interests of Africa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Nationalism
questions.a: Nationalism is a deep love and pride for one's country and the desire to see it free and self-governing.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Patriotism
questions.a: Patriotism is love for and loyalty to one's country, shown through good actions.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: A multiparty system of government
questions.a: A multiparty system is a system of government in which many political parties are allowed to compete for power.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Any four leading Pan-Africanists and their countries of origin.
questions.a: Any four of: Henry Sylvester Williams (Trinidad), W. E. B. Du Bois (America), Marcus Garvey (Jamaica), Booker T. Washington (America), Edward Blyden (Liberia), J. E. K. Aggrey (Ghana), Leopold Senghor (Senegal), Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana).

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Any four leading African nationalists and their countries.
questions.a: Any four of: Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana), Nnamdi Azikiwe (Nigeria), Hastings Kamuzu Banda (Malawi), Nelson Mandela (South Africa), Patrice Lumumba (D.R. Congo), Abdul Nasser (Egypt), Samora Machel (Mozambique), Julius Nyerere (Tanzania), Jomo Kenyatta (Kenya), Milton Obote (Uganda).

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Any four methods used by nationalists in the struggle for independence.
questions.a: Any four of: forming political parties, forming trade unions, organising strikes, boycotts, petitions and delegations, writing in newspapers, holding rallies, armed struggle.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Any four problems faced by nationalists.
questions.a: Any four of: death, imprisonment, detention, harsh laws, loss of property, intimidation, oppression, lack of funds, disunity, illiteracy among the people.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: The two African countries that were not colonised.
questions.a: Ethiopia and Liberia.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: The first country in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence and the year.
questions.a: Ghana, in 1957.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: The date Uganda got its independence.
questions.a: 9 October 1962.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: The battle in which Ethiopia defeated Italy.
questions.a: The Battle of Adowa (1896).

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: The city where the first Pan-African Conference was held.
questions.a: London.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Give four reasons why Africans wanted independence.
questions.a: Any four of: to control their national resources, to stop exploitation, to revive African culture, to regain land taken by settlers, to stop oppression, to gain social freedom and rights, to regain African dignity, to ensure human equality, to end racial discrimination.
accepted: to regain land taken by settlers
to gain social freedom and rights

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Give three reasons why Ethiopia was not colonised.
questions.a: It had a strong united government under Menelik II; it had modern weapons; its mountainous terrain made invasion difficult; the people were united by religion and history; it defeated Italy at Adowa in 1896. (Any three.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Give three advantages and three disadvantages of a single party system.
questions.a: Advantages: leadership is respected; there is less conflict; there is less rigging and few petitions; elections are cheaper; decisions are taken quickly. Disadvantages: it encourages dictatorship; there is less accountability; new ideas are not accepted; people have no choice of leaders; human rights may be abused. (Any three each.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Your school is choosing head prefects. Give two ways in which this election is like a multiparty election and two ways of making sure it is free and fair.
questions.a: Like a multiparty election: several candidates stand and campaign for the same post, and the pupils vote and choose the one they prefer. Making it free and fair: allow every candidate equal time to campaign; use a secret ballot; have neutral teachers or prefects count the votes in the open; announce the results publicly and allow complaints to be heard.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Why did the Second World War help to speed up the independence of African countries?
questions.a: African soldiers who fought in the war saw that Europeans were not superior, learnt to use modern weapons and returned with new ideas about freedom. The war also weakened the colonial powers economically, and the fight against dictatorship in Europe made it hard for the same powers to defend colonial rule. The United Nations, formed after the war, also encouraged self-rule.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Give two reasons why Pan-Africanists found it hard to unite Africa.
questions.a: Any two of: lack of unity and different political ideologies among the leaders; lack of enough funds; language barriers between English-speaking and French-speaking Africans; long distances between members; opposition and arrests by colonial governments.
accepted: lack of unity and different political ideologies among the leaders
language barriers between English-speaking and French-speaking Africans
opposition and arrests by colonial governments

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence of Africa
questions.q: Draw the map of Africa and shade Ethiopia, Liberia and Ghana. Label each one with what it is remembered for.
questions.a: Learner's map. Ethiopia — "never colonised, defeated Italy at Adowa 1896"; Liberia — "never colonised, home for freed slaves"; Ghana — "first in sub-Saharan Africa to be independent, 1957".

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: OAU
questions.a: OAU — the Organisation of African Unity.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: AU
questions.a: AU — the African Union.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: COMESA
questions.a: COMESA — the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: ECOWAS
questions.a: ECOWAS — the Economic Community of West African States.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Four objectives of the OAU.
questions.a: Any four of: to promote unity and solidarity of African states; to coordinate cooperation for a better life; to defend the independence and sovereignty of members; to remove all forms of colonialism from Africa; to promote international cooperation in line with the UN Charter.
accepted: to promote unity and solidarity of African states
to coordinate cooperation for a better life
to defend the independence and sovereignty of members
to remove all forms of colonialism from Africa
to promote international cooperation in line with the UN Charter

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Four organs of the AU.
questions.a: Any four of: the Assembly of Heads of State and Government, the Executive Council, the AU Commission, the Pan-African Parliament, the Peace and Security Council, the Court of Justice, ECOSOCC, the Permanent Representatives Committee.
accepted: the Assembly of Heads of State and Government

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Five regional economic groupings in Africa.
questions.a: EAC, COMESA, ECOWAS, SADC and IGAD.
accepted: EAC, COMESA, ECOWAS, SADC and IGAD.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Four member states of the East African Community.
questions.a: Any four of: Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, D.R. Congo, Somalia.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The date and place where the OAU was formed.
questions.a: 25 May 1963, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The number of founder members of the OAU.
questions.a: 32 member states.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The headquarters of the African Union.
questions.a: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The year the African Union was launched and the city where this happened.
questions.a: 2002, in Durban, South Africa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The day on which Africa Day is celebrated.
questions.a: 25 May.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give three achievements and three failures of the OAU.
questions.a: Achievements: it helped end colonialism in Africa; it helped end apartheid in South Africa; it solved some border conflicts such as Morocco and Algeria; it united Africa's voice; it gave birth to the AU. Failures: it failed to stop civil wars in Sudan, Somalia, Liberia and Rwanda; it failed to stop military coups; it failed to end poverty; it had limited funds; it could not interfere in members' internal affairs. (Any three each.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give four challenges facing the AU and two solutions to them.
questions.a: Challenges: limited funds; constant civil wars; different political ideologies; dependence on developed countries; poor governance and corruption; poor transport and communication. Solutions: members should pay their contributions on time; strengthen the Peace and Security Council; promote democracy and good governance; increase trade among African states. (Any four and any two.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give four advantages and three disadvantages of economic cooperation.
questions.a: Advantages: a wider market; free movement of people and goods; cheaper goods; joint projects; employment; peace and security; sharing of skills; stronger bargaining power. Disadvantages: loss of tax revenue; stronger members benefit more; spread of crime, smuggling and diseases; infant industries are killed by competition; loss of some independence; members produce similar goods. (Any four and any three.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A trader from Kampala sells maize in Kigali without paying import tax. Name the grouping that makes this possible and give two other benefits it brings to the trader.
questions.a: The East African Community (EAC). Other benefits: he can move freely and work in the other member states without difficulty; he reaches a much bigger market of customers; transport and border procedures are simpler and cheaper, and a common currency and standards are being worked on.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The EAC collapsed in 1977. Give two possible reasons why regional groupings break up and two things members can do to keep them alive.
questions.a: Reasons for breaking up: political differences and quarrels among leaders; unequal sharing of benefits, where one member gains more than the others; different economic systems and ideologies; wars and changes of government. Keeping them alive: share the benefits fairly and help weaker members; settle political differences peacefully through dialogue; honour agreements and pay contributions; build joint projects that all members own.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why does the African Union find it hard to stop wars in member states?
questions.a: Because it depends on member contributions and donor money, so it has limited funds for peacekeeping; because its old principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of members makes action difficult; because members have different interests and ideologies and do not always agree; and because some governments ignore AU decisions and there is little power to punish them.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw the map of Africa and shade the member states of the East African Community.
questions.a: Learner's map. Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, D.R. Congo and Somalia should be shaded.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A natural resource
questions.a: A natural resource is a resource provided by nature, such as land, water, minerals, vegetation, animals and climate.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Irrigation
questions.a: Irrigation is the supplying of water to crops artificially.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Nomadism
questions.a: Nomadism is the practice of moving from place to place with animals in search of pasture and water.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Brain drain
questions.a: Brain drain is the movement of skilled people out of a country to work in other countries.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The seven major economic resources of Africa.
questions.a: Land and soils, minerals, animals, people, vegetation, climate and water.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Four problems faced in the utilisation of resources in Africa.
questions.a: Any four of: low level of technology, shortage of capital, poor transport and communication, remote locations, political instability, over-exploitation, corruption, pollution, unreliable world prices.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Four ways of caring for our natural resources.
questions.a: Any four of: afforestation and reafforestation, crop rotation and terracing, controlled grazing, protecting wetlands and rivers, gazetting parks and reserves, recycling, public education, adding value to raw materials.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The six case-study countries in this topic and the main economic activity of each.
questions.a: Nigeria — oil drilling; Libya — oil mining and irrigation farming; Sudan — irrigation farming (cotton at Gezira); South Africa — mining and industry; D.R. Congo — mining and lumbering; Uganda — farming (coffee).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The main mineral mined in Libya.
questions.a: Oil (petroleum), together with natural gas.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The irrigation scheme found between the Blue Nile and the White Nile.
questions.a: The Gezira Irrigation Scheme.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The main crop grown in the Gezira Scheme.
questions.a: Cotton.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The dam built on the River Niger.
questions.a: The Kainji Dam.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The leading export crop of Uganda.
questions.a: Coffee.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give three social, three economic and three political challenges affecting economic development in Africa.
questions.a: Social: illiteracy, poverty, diseases, high mortality, famine, early marriages. Economic: poor transport, lack of capital, low technology, unemployment, corruption, brain drain. Political: wars and coups, political instability, refugees, poor governance. (Any three each.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why is South Africa the most industrialised country in Africa?
questions.a: Because it has plenty of minerals such as gold, coal, iron ore and platinum to feed its factories; it has capital and skilled labour; it has good transport and busy ports; it has plenty of electricity and a large market; and industries were developed there over a long period.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why must Libya use irrigation in order to farm?
questions.a: Because most of Libya lies in the Sahara Desert and receives less than 250 mm of rain a year. Without irrigation water from underground and from the Great Man-Made River, there would not be enough water for crops to grow.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Uganda exports raw coffee beans. Explain why processing the coffee before export would earn Uganda more money, and give two things needed to make this possible.
questions.a: Processing (roasting, grinding and packing) adds value, so the coffee sells at a much higher price than raw beans; it also creates jobs, saves the country from unstable raw-material prices and keeps the profit at home. To make this possible Uganda needs processing factories and reliable electricity, and skilled workers, capital and markets for the finished product.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give two ways in which being landlocked affects Uganda's trade and two solutions to the problem.
questions.a: Effects: goods take longer and cost more to reach the sea, which raises the price of imports and lowers the profit on exports; Uganda depends on the goodwill, roads and politics of neighbouring countries. Solutions: improve regional cooperation through the EAC so that transit is smooth; improve railway, road and air transport, use pipelines, and develop industries at home so that fewer heavy goods need to be imported.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A district has fertile soil but the people are still poor. Suggest three reasons and three solutions.
questions.a: Reasons: poor farming methods and low technology; lack of capital and credit; poor roads and no access to markets; small fragmented land holdings; crops sold raw and cheaply; lack of skills and education. Solutions: train farmers in modern methods; form cooperatives and provide credit; improve feeder roads and market information; add value by processing produce locally. (Any three each.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw the map of Africa and mark on it Nigeria, Sudan, South Africa and Uganda, writing the main economic activity of each.
questions.a: Learner's map. Nigeria — oil drilling; Sudan — irrigation farming (cotton); South Africa — mining and industry; Uganda — farming (coffee).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: UN
questions.a: UN — the United Nations.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: UNICEF
questions.a: UNICEF — the United Nations Children's Fund.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Human rights
questions.a: Human rights are the basic freedoms and entitlements that every person is born with.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: CHOGM
questions.a: CHOGM — the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The six main organs of the United Nations.
questions.a: The General Assembly, the Security Council, the Secretariat, the Economic and Social Council, the International Court of Justice and the Trusteeship Council.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The five permanent members of the Security Council.
questions.a: The United States of America, the United Kingdom, France, Russia and China.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any six agencies of the UN and one function of each.
questions.a: Any six, for example: UNESCO — education, science and culture; UNICEF — children's welfare; WHO — health and fighting diseases; ILO — workers' rights; UNDP — development projects; UNHCR — refugees; FAO — food and agriculture; WFP — food relief.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Any four functions of the Commonwealth of Nations.
questions.a: Any four of: promoting democracy and good governance; giving technical assistance and scholarships; promoting trade among members; settling disputes and observing elections; organising the Commonwealth Games; supporting small states.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The date the United Nations was formed.
questions.a: 24 October 1945.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The city where the UN headquarters is found.
questions.a: New York, in the United States of America.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The place where the International Court of Justice sits.
questions.a: The Hague, in the Netherlands.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The date the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted.
questions.a: 10 December 1948.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: The number of member countries of the Commonwealth.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Explain how the two world wars led to the formation of the United Nations.
questions.a: The First World War (1914–1918) caused terrible destruction, so the League of Nations was formed in 1919 to keep peace — but it was weak and failed to stop aggression. The Second World War (1939–1945) killed even more people and destroyed whole cities. The nations therefore met at San Francisco and formed a stronger organisation, the United Nations, in 1945, with a Security Council and peacekeeping powers, so that such wars would never happen again.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give four ways in which human rights are violated and four ways of respecting them.
questions.a: Violations: torture and inhuman punishment; detention without trial; child labour and child marriage; denying children education; discrimination; domestic violence; denying freedom of speech or worship. Respect: make and enforce protective laws; teach people their rights; set up human rights commissions and courts; give everyone a fair trial; provide education and health services; treat all people equally; report abuse. (Any four each.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give four challenges faced by the UN and the Commonwealth.
questions.a: Any four of: insecurity and political instability in member states; limited funding because members do not pay contributions; world dictators who ignore decisions; conflicts among member states; the veto power blocking UN decisions; decisions of the Commonwealth not being binding; domination by big powers.
accepted: insecurity and political instability in member states
limited funding because members do not pay contributions
the veto power blocking UN decisions
decisions of the Commonwealth not being binding

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: A school in your village receives desks, textbooks and a water tank from a UN agency. Name two agencies that could have done this and say what each one does.
questions.a: UNICEF — it provides for children's education, health, nutrition and protection, and often supplies desks, books and water facilities to schools. UNESCO — it promotes education, science and culture and supports schools with learning materials and teacher training. (UNDP or WFP would also be acceptable, with their correct work.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Compare the UN and the Commonwealth: give two similarities and two differences.
questions.a: Similarities: both promote peace, human rights and development; both give technical assistance and scholarships; both hold regular meetings of member states; Uganda is a member of both. Differences: the UN has 193 members from the whole world while the Commonwealth has 56, mostly former British territories; the UN has peacekeeping forces while the Commonwealth has none; the UN is headquartered in New York and the Commonwealth in London; UN Security Council decisions can be binding, while Commonwealth decisions depend on goodwill.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Some people say the veto power makes the Security Council unfair. Explain what the veto is and why people complain about it.
questions.a: The veto is the power held by each of the five permanent members of the Security Council — the USA, the UK, France, Russia and China — to block any decision, even when all the other members support it. People complain because it means one country can stop the whole world from acting, the five have not changed since 1945, Africa has no permanent seat, and important decisions about wars and peace can be blocked to protect a friend of one big power.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give three ways in which Uganda has benefited from the United Nations.
questions.a: Any three of: peacekeeping and support during conflicts; help for refugees through UNHCR; immunisation and health programmes through WHO and UNICEF; food relief through WFP and FAO; funding for schools, roads and other projects through UNDP and the World Bank; loans and economic advice from the IMF; scholarships and training for Ugandans.
accepted: immunisation and health programmes through WHO and UNICEF
food relief through WFP and FAO
roads and other projects through UNDP and the World Bank
loans and economic advice from the IMF
